title: Fundamental theorem for quantum asset pricing
abstract_summary: The paper studies a financial model where the market is described by a quantum pure state or density operator and introduces "quantum assets"—positive semidefinite operators whose payoffs depend on quantum states. It extends the notion of arbitrage to this setting and proves a quantum analogue of the first fundamental theorem of asset pricing: absence of arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of a risk-neutral density operator under which all assets are martingales, and it discusses a Radon–Nikodym-type measure change for density operators and illustrative examples.
methodology_description: This is a theoretical/mathematical study rather than an empirical/experimental one. The authors formulate a single-period financial market model in which the classical finite sample space is associated with the orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and market uncertainty is represented by a quantum density operator ρ on that Hilbert space. They introduce a new asset class ("quantum assets") defined as positive semidefinite Hermitian matrices whose payoffs are given by expectation values tr(ρS). The work develops an extended definition of arbitrage for portfolios when market states are quantum (and allows an optional subset of allowable states ˆH). They define discounted net gains Yi = Si/(1+r) − πi I and the notion of a risk-neutral (martingale) density operator ρ* satisfying πi = tr(ρ* Si/(1+r)). Mathematical tools and proof techniques include spectral decompositions, projector decomposition (Πnull, Π+), convex analysis and the separating hyperplane theorem, construction of convex sets of equivalent density operators, and a density-operator analogue of the Radon–Nikodym derivative implemented as a superoperator ϕ(σ,ρ)[·] = σ^{1/2} ρ^{-1/2} [·] ρ^{-1/2} σ^{1/2}. Using these formal constructs the authors prove a quantum analogue of the first fundamental theorem of asset pricing: absence of (quantum) arbitrage iff there exists an equivalent risk-neutral density operator. The methodology also includes simple illustrative two-dimensional (qubit / Pauli-basis) examples and a toy market-maker scenario to motivate the quantum-state market description. Full proofs and supporting lemmas are provided in appendices.

[speculative] It defines a new asset class, "quantum assets", modelled as positive semidefinite Hermitian matrices whose payoff in state |ψ> is ⟨ψ|S|ψ⟩.
[speculative] Classical assets are included as a special case by embedding classical payoff vectors as diagonal matrices in the same Hilbert space.
[speculative] The authors propose a definition of quantum arbitrage (Def. 3.1) appropriate to the density-operator market description and a set of allowable states.

[speculative] They show (Lemma B.1 and Corollary B.2) that arbitrage conditions can be characterised via discounted net-gain operators Y_i = S_i/(1+r) − π_i I, analogous to the classical net-gain approach.

[speculative] The main theoretical result is a quantum analogue of the First Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTQAP): a market model is quantum arbitrage-free if and only if there exists at least one risk-neutral density operator ρ* equivalent to the market density operator (Theorem 4.1).

[speculative] They define risk-neutral (martingale) density operators ρ* satisfying π_i = tr[ρ* S_i/(1+r)] for all traded assets, and show these operators can be used for arbitrage-free pricing of "quantum derivatives" via π_V = tr[ρ* V/(1+r)].

[speculative] The paper provides a density-operator analogue of the Radon–Nikodym derivative (a superoperator ϕ(σ,ρ)[·] = σ^{1/2} ρ^{-1/2}[·]ρ^{-1/2}σ^{1/2}) for changing between density operators and discusses basic properties of that map.

[speculative] Examples in 2×2 (qubit) systems illustrate that quantum coherence can (a) leave an arbitrage-free classical model arbitrage-free, (b) turn a classically arbitrage-free model into an arbitrage model when the allowable state set is extended, or (c) remove classical arbitrage depending on coherence and allowable-state choices.

[speculative] The authors provide a toy scenario motivating the model: a market maker using a quantum computation to determine future bid/ask prices, producing a market state ρ that market participants should consider when pricing/hedging.

[speculative] They note that pricing quantum derivatives (high-dimensional matrices) with risk-neutral density operators may be computationally challenging classically and could motivate use of quantum computers for pricing tasks.

[speculative] The work situates itself relative to prior literature on quantum extensions of stochastic calculus and previous quantum-finance connections (e.g., analogies between Black–Scholes and Schrödinger equations), but presents a distinct, density-operator based arbitrage/pricing theory.
results_summary: This theoretical preprint develops a formal framework for "quantum finance" in which the market is described by a quantum state (density operator) and traded assets are positive semidefinite Hermitian operators (quantum assets). The authors generalize arbitrage concepts to this setting, characterize arbitrage via discounted net-gain operators, and prove a quantum analogue of the first fundamental theorem of asset pricing: absence of arbitrage iff there exists an equivalent risk-neutral density operator. They define a Radon–Nikodym-type superoperator for density-operator measure change, propose a martingale pricing formula for quantum derivatives, and illustrate phenomena with simple qubit examples and a motivating toy scenario involving a quantum-computing market maker.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper suggests that quantum technologies could change market descriptions and that quantum computers may be needed to price high-dimensional quantum derivatives, but it provides theoretical formulations and examples only; no empirical or complexity-theoretic demonstration of practical quantum computational advantage is presented.
limitations: Single-period model: the paper studies a one-period (t=0,t=1) setting rather than multi-period markets (author-stated).
Examples limited to low dimension: the worked examples use 2×2 density operators; higher-dimensional behavior is not explored in the paper (author-stated).
Simplifying price assumption: bid and ask prices are assumed equal for simplicity (author-stated).

Undetermined existence/validity and intrinsic value of quantum assets: the paper introduces 'quantum assets' but explicitly leaves questions about their real-world existence/validity and intrinsic value for future work (author-stated).
Non-uniqueness of risk-neutral density operator: the risk-neutral density operator may not be unique (author-stated).
Single version of Radon–Nikodym derivative: the paper presents a particular density-operator Radon–Nikodym map and notes other forms/mechanisms might be needed (author-stated).
[inferred] Technological realism: the motivating toy scenario (market maker with a quantum computer preparing unmeasured quantum states) is idealized and may be difficult to realize in real markets.
[inferred] Market microstructure and operational details omitted: issues such as transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, market impact, clearing/settlement and regulatory constraints are not modeled.

[inferred] Measurement and timing subtleties: the treatment assumes an investor reasons about an unmeasured quantum state at t=1 from t=0, but practical implications of measurement back-action, information revelation timing, and coordination among market participants are not analyzed.
[inferred] Data and inference gap: the paper does not address how a real market participant would empirically estimate/learn the market density operator from prices or other data.

[inferred] Computational complexity and scalability: while the paper notes pricing in large-dimensional Hilbert spaces could require quantum computers, it does not analyze algorithmic complexity or provide resource estimates.

[inferred] Realizability of quantum assets as tradable instruments: although quantum assets are mathematically defined, practical mechanisms to issue, trade, transfer, and enforce payoffs tied to matrix-valued outcomes are not provided.

[inferred] Robustness to decoherence/noise: the framework assumes idealized quantum states/density operators; the effects of decoherence, noise, and imperfect devices on arbitrage and pricing are not addressed.
[inferred] Absence of empirical/experimental validation: no empirical examples, simulations tied to realistic market data, or experiments demonstrating the phenomena are provided.

contradictions: Quantum coherence can change arbitrage properties relative to classical embeddings: in simple qubit examples coherence can either create arbitrage where none existed classically or remove classical arbitrage depending on allowable-state choices. This contradicts any naive expectation that embedding a classical market into the quantum formalism will always preserve classical arbitrage properties.
